tone: Primarily lighthearted and fun — dorm life, rivalries, chaos, friendship, competition — with genuine dramatic stakes that escalate through each tier. The comedy and the tragedy earn each other. Season 1 ends with the class intact but the world more complicated than it was.

tiers.title: Welcome to U.A.
tiers.overall_tone: Almost entirely fun. This is orientation. The class is meeting each other, figuring out who they are, discovering the school is hard and also ridiculous. Everyone in Tokyo knows the name Ruin — a small, dangerous villain group that's been running Kurogane Wharf for years. Fracture, the anti-licensing movement getting louder across the city, is a completely separate thing — though nobody knows that yet. None of it has touched the class directly, and Undertow himself is still just a name on a rumor.
tiers.dm_at_a_glance: U.A.'s campus in Tier 1 still feels new — hallways nobody has memorized yet, a dorm kitchen nobody's claimed territory in. The class is twenty strangers figuring out who's actually dangerous and who just looks it. Ruin exists at the edge of things: a name on a news ticker, something Fujisaki mentions and moves past, graffiti near Kurogane Wharf nobody in the class has been to yet. Nobody says the word "Undertow" — it hasn't been said yet, by anyone. When things go wrong here, they go wrong the way a bad dorm fire drill goes wrong: loud, red-faced, survivable. Chozen's Stress spiking during the entrance exam isn't a crisis, it's the first time his classmates see him flinch. Toshida cratering a wall mid-panic gets him a look from Fujisaki, not a lecture. This tier is twenty specific people finding out what they're actually like under pressure.

arcs.name: The Entrance Exam
arcs.dm_goal: The exam starts with no warning and no plan — drones hatch, a wall comes down, civilian actors start shouting, and twenty strangers have to decide in real time whether to work together or not. Oshiro is quietly grading the cooperation instinct. What the table actually gets is better: who reaches for the wall Toshida just leveled, who's already gone before anyone registers Ren moved, whose first instinct under real pressure surprises even them.
arcs.description: A staged disaster scenario in a simulated city block. Students must rescue civilians (actors and prop mannequins) while combat drones provide the villain opposition. No predetermined groupings — everyone is on their own. This is how the class meets each other.
beats: Opening chaos: the exam starts without warning — no countdown, no announcement. Students scatter and self-organise in real time. Ren is simply gone mid-sprint; nobody sees him move.

Key moments: Toshida shouts a word and levels a wall segment. Nakaya jump-starts a stalled bus's dead battery with a controlled arc to use it as a ramp, then can't get the engine to switch off. Chozen's Stress activates on its own in round one — it doesn't need his permission, and the noise and chaos are enough to trigger a small, unwanted spike before he's decided to fight anything.
Conflict point: Masahata loudly critiques everyone else's technique mid-exam. He's correct about roughly half of it, which makes it worse.
Drone boss: the final obstacle is a single large combat drone targeting the highest-scoring candidates. Students have to cooperate — or use each other as distractions — to bring it down.
Resolution: the class passes collectively. Score rankings post. Masahata reads them twice. The ranking chart era begins.

villain_seeds.fracture: Graffiti on the arena's exterior wall during student arrival: 'HEROES SERVE COMMISSIONS, NOT COMMUNITIES' in the jagged-line Fracture style. Weathered enough to have been there for weeks. Nobody on the exam staff comments on it.
villain_seeds.null_signal: A compact black drone with no UA markings logged the exam from the upper observation tier. The exam team assumed it was another faculty member's equipment. It was not in the manifest. No footage was flagged.
villain_seeds.the_chain: Absent from direct play. A single offhand comment from an agency worker at the venue gates: 'Avoid Kurogane Wharf after dark this week. Ruin's been busy lately.' Said the way you'd mention traffic. Nobody asks a follow-up question.

arcs.name: Dorm Life & Combat Training
arcs.type: Social arc + first formal training encounter
arcs.dm_goal: This is the class figuring out who's who once the exam adrenaline wears off — burnt rice, a short-circuited toaster nobody will own up to, Masahata's ranking chart appearing on the fridge unasked. Capture the Flag turns that same energy competitive: Oshiro splits teams so nobody fights their obvious counter, and the matchups are where rivalries stop being vibes and start being specific grudges. Nothing here is dangerous. It's just the first time the class looks like a class.
arcs.description: The class moves into Heights Alliance. First week is pure character chaos — personalities collide, routines form, the common room becomes a social ecosystem. Oshiro's opening combat class (Capture the Flag) runs in the second session: two teams, live stakes, no mercy.
beats: The doorframe incident (Toshida, day one): a word escapes him mid-yawn. A panel falls out of the doorframe. He apologises and fixes it. The panel falls again the next morning. He has quietly named the doorframe Hiroshi and considers this an ongoing rivalry.

The charger incident (Nakaya, day two): she jump-starts Masahata's dead phone charger with a small controlled arc, purely as a favor. It works, technically. It also fuses the charging port shut permanently at roughly double voltage. She considers this an unambiguous success.

Masahata prints and laminates a ranking chart based on exam scores. It appears on the fridge, fully formatted with tier brackets. No one asked him to do this. Kinosho stares at it for a long time and says nothing.

Capture the Flag — Oshiro's opening combat class: team assignments calibrated for discomfort, not balance. Yoshibara immediately doubles herself — Oshiro rules it legal because he didn't say it wasn't. Kinosho predicted this exact outcome days ago, told no one, purely to test a hypothesis about whether anyone would believe her if she had. Ando loses to someone he was certain he'd beat and wears his sunglasses for the next 36 hours including during sleep.
Masahata updates the ranking chart to include 'combat performance (preliminary).' No methodology is explained. It is accurate.

Cafeteria crossover: Class 1-B eats on the same schedule. First real contact is small and unremarkable — a shared table because the room is full, Matsunami's class visibly running a tighter ship than Oshiro's. No rivalry yet, just the first time 1-A registers there's another class exactly like them, a hallway away.

villain_seeds.fracture: A leaflet appears under a dorm door on day three. Black print, spare design, jagged-line symbol. 'Your quirk is yours — not your license.' Someone pushed it through. Nobody saw who.
villain_seeds.null_signal: If any student explores Hamagawa's open-door office in the evening, a monitor in standby shows a file header before the screensaver kicks in: 'Provisional License Cohort Data — External Access Request, Ref: SA/7-91.' Requesting party: 'Seika Advanced Systems.' The file is already closed when they look.
villain_seeds.the_chain: The common room TV runs news in the background one evening. Kurogane Wharf. A small support agency for unlicensed quirk users has closed 'due to changing neighbourhood conditions.' The report is twelve seconds long.

arcs.name: The Agency Visit
arcs.dm_goal: First time outside the walls without exam conditions telling them what's safe. Patchwork treats the actual villain encounter like a Tuesday; the students don't. Ruin stops being a name on a news ticker and becomes a tag on a warehouse door, a delivery schedule that doesn't add up, a face Hardskin won't explain. Fracture's presence is in the same neighborhood at the same time — a flyer, a chant two streets over — and nothing connects the two out loud. A player who's paying attention notices. Nobody points it out for them.
arcs.description: The class assists at Patchwork Agency in Kurogane Wharf for a day. Filing, crowd management at a public event, basic patrol. Their first taste of actual hero work. Mostly administrative and slightly boring. A minor incident near the end brings the class's first real Ruin encounter — and if students are paying attention, a Ruin researcher and a Fracture marker are also present in the margins.
beats: Arrival: the agency is underwhelmed by having twenty students in their breakroom simultaneously. They did not fully plan for this.
Aikawa organises an entire filing system the agency didn't ask for. It is objectively better than what they had. They are mildly resentful.
Crowd management at a small community event. Toshida is stationed away from the speakers. This is communicated very clearly. He is stationed near the speakers anyway due to a logistical mix-up.

The incident: two Ruin Grunts and a Ruin Hardskin are intimidating a shopkeeper in a side street. The class has six seconds before Patchwork arrives. Decision point: wait or intervene. Both choices are defensible. The Hardskin's fear when contained — not of the students, but of being seen by them — is the most important data in the encounter.

Patchwork's debrief: direct, accurate, slightly alarming. She's been watching since they arrived. 'The quiet one — that's not local. You walked into someone's business trip.' She won't say more today. She makes a quiet call after they leave.

villain_seeds.the_chain: The Hardskin has a chain-link tattoo visible on DC 15 Perception during the fight, DC 12 on a subdued target. His fear of being identified is disproportionate for a low-level criminal caught by student heroes. That gap is the important data. Patchwork says 'affiliated' once and doesn't elaborate.
villain_seeds.null_signal: Ryo Karashi ('Splice') appears in a corridor inside Patchwork Agency. Visitor badge: 'Seika Consulting — Dr. R. Karashi.' Slim tablet, unhurried, claims wrong floor. If stopped: warm, apologetic, gives nothing away. The tablet, if glimpsed, shows a student photo grid — the class's entrance exam publicity shots. He is gone in thirty seconds.
villain_seeds.fracture: The Fracture jagged-line symbol is scratched into the concrete of the alley wall behind where the Ruin Hardskin was standing. Old enough to be weathered — months, not weeks. Not a message placed for today. A marker. Someone was using this alley before Ruin was.

tiers.villain_presence: Ruin is background texture in Tier 1. Its street-level side is the most visible — one direct encounter with low-tier operatives, planted through a pro hero's offhand comment. Its research side is glimpsed twice: the unmarked exam drone, Splice's thirty-second corridor appearance. Fracture — a separate movement — is found rather than encountered: graffiti, a leaflet, a symbol scratched in concrete. Nobody from Ruin has spoken to the class directly yet, and Undertow himself hasn't shown his face to anyone — that starts in Tier 2.

tiers.title: Getting Good
tiers.overall_tone: The Sports Festival is peak chaos and excitement — the class gets to show off and it is almost entirely fun. Then the world gets complicated: Fracture becomes a real moral problem the class can't punch away, and the Convergence finale puts Kuma's logistics run, one of Null's extraction teams, and a Fracture sabotage crew in the same Kurogane Wharf warehouse on the same night — Ruin's own people not coordinating with each other, and Fracture not coordinating with anyone but themselves. Season 1 ends with a win that doesn't feel entirely clean, and Undertow walking out of a fight he was never really in.
tiers.dm_at_a_glance: Three arcs, three different colors. The Sports Festival is stadium lights and a live crowd — every match in the bracket below is written as a specific rivalry, not a stat comparison. The Fracture Problem puts Shard in front of the class with real, uncomfortable arguments about the licensing system — she believes every word of it, and has no idea that a chunk of Fracture's funding traces back to Ruin, the group she insists has nothing to do with her movement. Convergence is Ruin's own operation and Fracture's sabotage crew colliding in the same warehouse on the same night, neither side expecting the other. Kuma is the fight the class can't talk their way out of. Splice is the wrinkle nobody predicted. Undertow is a shape in a doorway as everyone else is still catching their breath — seen, not caught. The class walks out having won the room. Season 2 is what happens when they go looking for the man who wasn't in it.

arcs.name: The Sports Festival
arcs.dm_goal: Stadium lights, a real crowd, Masahata's chart getting updated in real time from the stands. Every match in the bracket below is written as two specific people, not two quirks — Yamaru absorbing four clean Impacts from Toragi before he finally goes down, because his whole Quirk is refusing to register how much that should have hurt, Chozen's win feeling too big for the arena because it's damage he can't undo, not a triumphant finish. Play PC fights out in full. NPC fights get one paragraph, read aloud, and then the class's reaction to what they just watched.
arcs.description: U.A.'s annual Sports Festival. Public, broadcast, massive audience. Full tournament structure: obstacle race → cavalry battle → individual brackets with Class 1-B competing alongside Class 1-A. The 1-A vs 1-B rivalry becomes concrete here for the first time.
beats: Pre-festival: the class arrives to a stadium already full. Kazama is recognised from the entrance exam footage and loses his composure for about four seconds — long enough for someone to notice his ears go red before the mirror-bright hardening kicks in and hides it.

Obstacle race: Zaro wins her heat by portaling ahead through gaps nobody else could see, fog trailing behind her the whole way — nobody realised how far ahead she was until the leaderboard updated. Ren places first overall; nobody saw him pass anyone, he was just suddenly at the front. Setaka's iron cannon-balls ricochet through a bottleneck and eliminate four competitors at once, and he apologises to each of them individually afterward. Kinosho places top five in a near-sleep state for most of the course. Yamaru Todao (1-B) places third — the class's first look at him in a competitive context.

Cavalry battle: alliances form and collapse. Class 1-B's coordination is visibly drilled and slightly alarming to watch. Yoshibara doubles the wrong person at the wrong moment — an opponent already in the lead. This becomes a permanent campaign reference.

Broadcast: the commentary team is unprepared for half the quirks on display. 'What Is She Doing?' about Kinosho trends nationally within twenty minutes. Masahata's ongoing scoring commentary in the waiting room is caught on a spectator's phone and briefly goes viral.
Post-festival: the ranking chart, brought to the festival laminated, doesn't get updated for four days. When asked why: 'The model is broken.' He reprints it anyway.

event_1_obstacle_race.summary: All participants, mixed classes. Results seed the individual brackets.
key_moments: Zaro portals through gaps nobody else could see, fog trailing the whole route
Ren places 1st overall — nobody saw him pass anyone
Setaka's iron balls ricochet through a bottleneck and eliminate four at once, apologies included
Kinosho places top 5 in a near-sleep state for most of the course
Yamaru Todao (1-B) places 3rd — Class 1-A has had his exam score on the fridge chart since week one

event_2_cavalry_battle.summary: Teams of 4. Collect headbands. Top 16 advance to individual brackets.
key_moments: Yoshibara doubles herself mid-battle, then doubles the wrong person — an opponent already in the lead. Her double and the lead-holder collide centre-arena. Scoring briefly favours the class before correcting.
Class 1-B's coordination is surgical, drilled, and slightly alarming to watch.
Kinosho's team doesn't appear to be coordinating at all. They place 3rd anyway. Nobody can explain how.

event_3_individual_tournament.format: 16 competitors, mixed 1-A and 1-B. Top 4 seeded. Single elimination.

seeds.name: Ren Suzuki
seeds.note: 1st in the obstacle race. The class has been watching him move. Nobody knows what his speed looks like in a direct fight yet.

seeds.name: Yamaru Todao
seeds.note: 3rd in the obstacle race. Quiet about being on the fridge chart. Thinking about it too.

seeds.name: Chozen Tadachi
seeds.note: Placed well across both events despite Stress not being a movement quirk — his obstacle finish was pure discipline.

seeds.name: Kagamo Akake
seeds.note: Palm Cannon blasts felt across the arena in the cavalry battle. She was in a different quadrant entirely.

round_1.how_it_goes: A slow, technical fight the crowd wasn't primed for. Kazama hardens immediately and closes; Isosato answers by compressing a wall directly in his path, buying a full round while it solidifies. For two rounds he's grinding through fresh constructs almost as fast as she can raise them. Kazama switches to Steel Weapon strikes and starts timing his hits for the moment a wall is still soft — punching clean through the third one before it sets, and closing the gap before she can raise a fourth.
round_1.dm_note: Play this as a genuine technical standoff, not a spectacle fight. If PC, let the player feel the grind — Isosato's constructs ticking down almost as fast as she raises them, Kazama's hardening uses burning faster than any other R1 fight costs him.

alternate_outcome.how_it_goes: Isosato reads Kazama's timing and starts leaving walls a half-second longer in their soft state on purpose — he commits to a strike that punches through empty air as the real wall solidifies a foot further back than he expected. Round 3, he's boxed into a corridor of his own hardened footprints with nowhere left to charge from.
alternate_outcome.downstream: Isosato advances to QF-3 instead of Kazama. Chozen's escalation curve into QF-3 shifts slightly — he still wins, just quieter, against someone who never intended to trade damage with him directly.
alternate_outcome.dm_note: Kazama watching from the stands for the rest of the tournament is a real beat. He doesn't leave.

round_1.how_it_goes: Toshida's Comic shout disrupts Toragi's first Twin Impact — the timing breaks, a genuine near-upset. She absorbs it and shuts him down methodically on the second attempt. The crowd goes silent three seconds, then very loud.
round_1.dm_note: Let the first Impact failing surprise people. The second win is inevitable but shouldn't feel like it in the moment.

alternate_outcome.how_it_goes: His second disruption lands better than either of them expected. Toragi runs out of prepared responses. Toshida wins by surviving to the end of her playbook.
alternate_outcome.downstream: Toshida advances to QF-2 vs Yamaru — a shout can't disrupt something that was never relying on timing to begin with. Yamaru wins QF-2 cleanly.
alternate_outcome.dm_note: Toragi watching Yamaru beat Toshida with none of the disruption that beat her is worth a beat. She writes something down.

round_1.how_it_goes: Kinosho deactivates Aikawa's iron claws mid-swing, walks up to her, and it's over in about forty seconds. Her eyes flatten to that dull pewter grey for a second when Neutralization triggers — the crowd doesn't understand what happened. 'What Is She Doing?' trends within the hour.
round_1.dm_note: Don't explain the win to the audience — the commentary team can't either. Masahata looks at the chart, says nothing, sits down.

alternate_outcome.how_it_goes: Neutralization needs a targeting window — the right limb, a moment to close. Aikawa's claws are too fast and varied to give her one. Aikawa lands the hit Kinosho didn't expect, because Kinosho's plan assumed a window that never opened.
alternate_outcome.downstream: Aikawa advances to QF-4 vs Kagamo. Palm Cannon blasts don't care about claws — ranged force beats her close-in strikes before she can close the gap. Kagamo wins.
alternate_outcome.dm_note: Kinosho watching from the stands afterward is very quiet. She's studying something specific in every subsequent fight.

round_1.how_it_goes: Ando's scales shrug off the first engine-charge clean. Izuto clocks it and times his second burst for the moment Ando's mid-pivot repositioning. Ando goes down surprised. Sunglasses stay on for the rest of the day, through the surprise and everything after — he will not let anyone see whatever his face did in that half-second.
round_1.dm_note: Ando's first shrug should feel definitive. Izuto's adjustment is the character beat — problem-solver under pressure, same instinct he uses maintaining his own leg-engines.

alternate_outcome.how_it_goes: Izuto's plan needed a third move Ando was already braced for — he read the adjustment coming and shrugged the second charge the same way as the first. Ando wins by being less complicated than expected.
alternate_outcome.downstream: Ando advances to QF-1 vs Ren. Scales can't block what he can't track — Ren wins, less cleanly than the Izuto fight.
alternate_outcome.dm_note: Izuto watching Ren beat Ando is worth playing — he's cataloguing footwork, not emoting about the loss.

round_1.how_it_goes: Zaro drops a shroud of deep purple fog around herself before the opening bell and puts a portal down at the arena's far edge. Ren wins in eleven seconds — he crossed the arena faster than the introduction finished, arriving at the portal's mouth before she'd finished routing anything through it. Her plan assumed her opponent needed to find the portal first. He didn't look for it; he just arrived. The crowd replays the footage three times trying to find the contact point.
round_1.dm_note: Run this as a demonstration, not a fight. The class should clock that Zaro had a real plan and it simply didn't matter — Ren's own private tally of 'things that should have stopped me' gets a new entry he'll never admit counts. Zaro is a PC — if a player is running her, let this be about her plan being sound and the outcome not being humiliating, just outpaced.

alternate_outcome.how_it_goes: She opens a second, closer portal she never announced, and steps through it the instant Ren commits to the first one. Ren's eleven-second plan assumes a location she isn't at anymore. He overshoots; in the half-second he's reorienting, she lands the hit nobody saw coming from behind the fog.
alternate_outcome.downstream: MAJOR UPSET — Ren eliminated Round 1. Zaro advances to QF-1 vs Izuto, who reads her portal placement through the way the fog thins right before she opens one, and wins.
alternate_outcome.dm_note: The class's reaction to Ren losing matters more than the fight. Masahata does not update the chart for a long time.

round_1.how_it_goes: Yoshibara doubles immediately — standard opening, both copies committing to hits at once. Yamaru just takes both. Neither lands anything close to what would actually put him down, and he doesn't bother guessing which one's real before responding to both in turn. She tries four more doubles across three rounds; every hit registers, none of them change the fight. First definitive 1-B win of the tournament, and one of the least dramatic-looking ones.
round_1.dm_note: Yoshibara is genuinely doing everything right — the doubling works exactly as designed. It just isn't enough damage against someone whose whole Quirk is absorbing exactly this kind of accumulating pressure. Post-fight, she looks at her hands, shrugs. Respects it more than she expected to.

alternate_outcome.how_it_goes: She and her double land enough consecutive hits, fast enough, that Yamaru's hidden threshold gets crossed before either of them realises how close it was — he goes down suddenly, mid-sentence, with no visible warning beforehand.
alternate_outcome.downstream: Yoshibara advances to QF-2 vs Toragi. Twin Impact doesn't care how much punishment an opponent can already absorb — it detonates where it's placed. Toragi wins QF-2 cleanly.
alternate_outcome.dm_note: Yamaru watching Yoshibara lose to Toragi afterward, from the stands, entirely unbothered — he clocks exactly what beat him and files it away without comment.

round_1.how_it_goes: Hashige reshapes the arena's scattered metal fixtures into a full restraining lattice in four seconds — every movement tracked, a wall raised, a set of cuffs half-formed and waiting. Chozen isn't trying to evade any of it — he's simply already absorbed two rounds of solid hits from a tournament fight, and his Stress percentage is climbing off real accumulated damage, not nerves. Round 2, Hashige has to choose between holding the lattice or getting clear; he holds. Chozen walks through it anyway — the damage he's already banked from landing blows is enough on its own. The restraints register contact and buckle. Hashige loses a tactically sound fight because the math changed mid-fight.
round_1.dm_note: Hashige didn't make a mistake — acknowledge that in the commentary. Chozen's rising damage percentage is the variable his model didn't have room for. If PC, this is banked damage becoming a resource, not stress-as-vibes.

alternate_outcome.how_it_goes: This is only Chozen's first fight of the day — his Stress percentage hasn't had time to build from actual damage taken yet. The lattice locks him down completely before he's banked enough hits to break through it.
alternate_outcome.downstream: Hashige advances to QF-3 vs Kazama. His metal control is built to restrain evasive fighters, not someone who hardens and simply walks through the lines. Kazama wins, the restraints snapping audibly.
alternate_outcome.dm_note: Chozen watching Hashige's technique from the stands afterward — cataloguing, not sulking.

round_1.how_it_goes: Domoto kicks off to a safe position on the far side of the arena; Kagamo's first Palm Cannon blast hits the whole quadrant at once. Domoto bursts again to a new landing spot; the second blast tells her there are no safe landing spots left in range. She thinks about it for a genuine moment, then raises her hand. Kagamo looks mildly disappointed it ended there.
round_1.dm_note: Domoto's pause before surrendering is doing the math, not giving up. Kagamo wanted a harder problem.

alternate_outcome.how_it_goes: She reads the third blast's wind-up and kicks off directly into Kagamo's personal space instead of away from it — too close for a Palm Cannon to aim properly. Neither of them planned for close range. She wins on improvisation, visibly bewildered by her own success.
alternate_outcome.downstream: Domoto advances to QF-4 vs Kinosho, who simply deactivates the Rabbit Quirk's burst mid-jump. Kinosho wins.
alternate_outcome.dm_note: Kagamo watching Kinosho work is a quiet beat — genuinely curious, not sore about the loss.

quarterfinals.note: Fighter B is whoever won R1-4 (default Izuto; Ando if alt R1-4; Zaro takes the slot if she upset Ren in R1-5, in which case fighter A becomes Zaro)
quarterfinals.how_it_goes: The fastest fight of the tournament. Izuto has been clocking Ren's movement since the entrance exam and built a three-move plan; he gets through two. Ren wins. Izuto is already thinking about the third move he didn't land — the same methodical instinct he uses maintaining his own leg components.
quarterfinals.dm_note: If PC, let Izuto's plan get close to working — the fun is how near he comes, not Ren dominating.

alternate_outcome.how_it_goes: This time he gets all three moves through, the third accounting for exactly how Ren decelerates before contact. Izuto wins, already dissatisfied — thinking about what a fourth move would look like.
alternate_outcome.downstream: Izuto advances to SF-1 vs Toragi. Her dodge-corridor trick worked on Ren's readable pattern; Izuto's is adaptive, so she needs longer to find an answer. She wins SF-1, but it's her hardest fight of the tournament.
alternate_outcome.dm_note: Post-fight: Ren finds Izuto. 'The third move.' 'Yes.' That's the whole conversation.

quarterfinals.note: Fighter B is whoever won R1-2 (default Toragi; Toshida if alt R1-2). Fighter A is whoever won R1-6 (default Yamaru; Yoshibara if alt R1-6)
quarterfinals.how_it_goes: Best fight of the quarterfinals. Toragi's first Twin Impact lands clean — full detonation, textbook placement. Nobody's shrugged it off like this before. She adjusts, escalates, lands a second and a third. Yamaru is still standing. By the fourth exchange the crowd has stopped waiting for him to go down and started waiting to find out if he can.
quarterfinals.dm_note: Toragi's technique is genuinely flawless here — this isn't a fight she loses through error, it's a fight Yamaru survives through sheer accumulated threshold, right up until he doesn't. Post-fight: Yamaru approaches. 'Your Impact timing. Never seen anyone land four clean.' 'I know.' He nods. The beginning of mutual respect.

alternate_outcome.how_it_goes: Toragi's fourth Impact is the one meant to finally close it out — it lands exactly where she wants. Yamaru's threshold holds by a margin neither of them can see from the outside. He's still standing when she runs out of prepared follow-ups.
alternate_outcome.downstream: Yamaru advances to SF-1 vs Ren, who's too fast for a straightforward war of attrition and wins on pure speed before Yamaru's endurance becomes relevant.
alternate_outcome.dm_note: The class watching a 1-B student reach the final matters for the rivalry dynamic. Masahata's chart has been updated three times by now.

quarterfinals.note: Fighter A is whoever won R1-7 (default Chozen; Hashige if alt R1-7). Fighter B is whoever won R1-1 (default Kazama; Isosato if alt R1-1)
quarterfinals.how_it_goes: Kazama does exactly what Steel wants — close, harden, trade. But every exchange he lands and takes both feed Chozen's rising damage percentage the same way any accumulating hit would; there's no range to retreat to the way a blaster could use. By round 4, Chozen is hitting harder than Kazama's shell was built to take in one sitting. Steel shatters two rounds earlier than Kazama expected.
quarterfinals.dm_note: First time the stadium sees Chozen properly escalated — run round 4 as genuinely alarming. Kazama's loss should feel unfair in a way that's hard to articulate: he did exactly what his quirk is for and the accumulated damage simply outpaced his absorption cap.

alternate_outcome.how_it_goes: Kazama commits everything to Steel Weapon in the first thirty seconds, before Chozen's damage percentage has climbed anywhere near its threshold. Round 1 Chozen is manageable. Kazama wins before round 3.
alternate_outcome.downstream: Kazama advances to SF-2 vs Kinosho, who deactivates his Steel mid-harden. His trained physical technique underneath is real but not enough unarmored. Kinosho wins after four rounds.
alternate_outcome.dm_note: The crowd wanted spectacle and got a clean, quiet win instead. Kazama isn't sure how to feel about winning by being less than what people came to see.

quarterfinals.note: Fighter A is whoever won R1-8 (default Kagamo; Domoto if alt R1-8). Fighter B is whoever won R1-3 (default Kinosho; Aikawa if alt R1-3)
quarterfinals.how_it_goes: Kagamo's blasts are pure kinetic force at range — Neutralization can't deactivate something that's already left her hands as displaced air. Her first plan fails visibly. Her second plan is assembling something from arena debris mid-fight; Kagamo ends up briefly airborne, caught by a contraption Kinosho built in forty seconds. She doesn't have a construction quirk. Nobody asks how she did it.
quarterfinals.dm_note: Kagamo afterward: 'I don't know what she did.' Genuinely interested, not embarrassed.

alternate_outcome.how_it_goes: Kinosho's contraption holds for thirty seconds; a second Palm Cannon blast dismantles it from underneath before the third component locks in. She concedes.
alternate_outcome.downstream: Kagamo advances to SF-2 vs Chozen (or Kazama). Against Chozen, the arena chaos and accumulated fight damage feed his escalation and he wins. Against Kazama, her blasts keep breaking his footing before Steel Weapon can close the gap, and Kagamo wins.
alternate_outcome.dm_note: 'What Is She Doing?' never airs a second segment. The silence where it would've been is its own thing.

semifinals.note: Fighter A is whoever won QF-1. Fighter B is whoever won QF-2. Default path is Ren vs Toragi.
semifinals.how_it_goes: UPSET. Twin Impact's first hit is a decoy placed on a predicted dodge corridor. Ren dodges exactly as expected; the real Impact triggers on the dodge vector itself. He can't outrun something aimed at where he's going rather than where he is. He loses a very fast fight that shocks everyone including him.
semifinals.dm_note: Post-fight: Ren finds Toragi. 'The second hit.' 'Yes.' Two sentences, complete understanding. Don't add to it.

alternate_outcome.how_it_goes: He clocks the dodge-corridor placement and simply doesn't dodge — takes the first Impact and wins through it. Toragi has no contingency for someone who isn't trying to avoid it.
alternate_outcome.downstream: Ren advances to the Final vs Chozen. Speed against escalation — he needs to end it by round 2 or Chozen's accumulated damage becomes a different problem entirely.
alternate_outcome.dm_note: A Ren vs Chozen final has completely different energy than Toragi vs Chozen.

semifinals.note: Fighter A is whoever won QF-3. Fighter B is whoever won QF-4. Default path is Chozen vs Kinosho.
semifinals.how_it_goes: Kinosho neutralizes Chozen's quirk directly. But Neutralization suppresses the label, not the damage percentage he's already banked from two prior escalating fights today — and any hit that still lands while the quirk is down just keeps that percentage climbing underneath the suppression. She deactivates what she can reach. What's already accumulated keeps feeding itself. Chozen wins, visibly running hot on the way out of the arena.
semifinals.dm_note: This is entirely a damage-accumulation mechanic, not an ambient-stress one — Chozen's own sheet is explicit that only actual damage taken raises his Stress percentage. Kinosho can suppress the quirk's active use but not undo banked damage. His win should feel slightly worrying, not triumphant.

alternate_outcome.how_it_goes: She keeps landing precise, minimal hits that end exchanges before they add real damage to his total, denying him the accumulation he needs. The suppression holds because there's nothing new feeding it. She closes the window before it reopens.
alternate_outcome.downstream: Kinosho advances to the Final vs Toragi. Two methodical fighters at their actual ceiling. Kinosho wins on round four when Toragi's timing becomes readable.
alternate_outcome.dm_note: Run a Kinosho vs Toragi final as the quietest possible ending — no commentary noise, just the two of them and a crowd slowly realising it's already over.

third_place.note: Fighters are the two SF losers. Default is Ren vs Kinosho.
third_place.how_it_goes: Ren wins. Says nothing about it after. Kinosho seems to find this appropriate. Masahata notes the result and adds a column titled 'semantic outcomes' to the chart. Nobody asks him what this means.

alternate_outcome.how_it_goes: Kinosho wins. Ren loses cleanly and accepts it cleanly — one nod. Masahata adds 'semantic outcomes: confirmed.'
alternate_outcome.dm_note: Run whichever result serves the table emotionally — a win for Ren after a brutal SF loss, or a definitive close for Kinosho's arc.

final.note: Fighters are the two SF winners. Default is Toragi vs Chozen.
final.favored: Toragi — technically superior, has beaten 1-B's seed 2, has a plan for Chozen's escalation curve
final.how_it_goes: Toragi's plan: end it before he escalates. She lands the cleanest technical strike of the tournament in the opening exchange. It is the worst decision she could have made — Chozen has already fought two escalating rounds today, his damage percentage already elevated before this fight even started, and her perfect hit just adds directly to a total that was never at zero. The fight drags to round 5. Nobody predicted round 5. It ends when his accumulated total exceeds anything her technique can counter.
final.dm_note: Toragi's plan is visibly correct until the moment the math changes on her. Chozen's win should feel too big for the arena — overwhelming, not triumphant. Give him the quiet moment coming down while the crowd is still loud.

alternate_outcome.how_it_goes: She waits instead of committing immediately — lets him start to build, then closes the window with a second strike before it climbs further. Wins in round 2.
alternate_outcome.downstream: Toragi wins the Sports Festival. The commentary calls it 'flawless'; she privately disagrees with the word — she won because her preparation was better, and that's a different thing.
alternate_outcome.dm_note: Null, watching the broadcast, takes specific interest in Toragi's precision — better footage of her technique than the exam drone ever captured.

post_tournament_moments: Yamaru finds Toragi after QF-2. 'Your Impact timing. Never seen anyone land four clean.' 'I know.' Both write it down.
Ren finds Toragi after SF-1. 'The second hit.' 'Yes.' He thinks about it for the rest of the campaign.

Kazama's stalemate against Isosato in R1-1 becomes the slowest, most talked-about fight of the day. Someone sends him a photo of the two of them locked mid-fight, a half-solidified wall between them. He never shows it to anyone.
'What Is She Doing?' about Kinosho airs twice. She watches both replays alone in the waiting room, satisfied.
Kagamo, after losing to Kinosho: 'I don't know what she did.' Genuinely interested. Masahata writes it down immediately.
The ranking chart — brought to the festival laminated — doesn't get updated for four days. 'The model is broken.' He reprints it anyway.

villain_seeds.all_factions: Ruin is watching the Sports Festival broadcast like the rest of Tokyo. Null is collecting comprehensive quirk activation data — better footage than the exam drone captured. Fracture, completely separately, is watching because the festival represents exactly the system they oppose: licensed quirk use as public spectacle. Undertow watches Chozen's final with specific interest — the only person in Tokyo tracking both angles at once. None of this is visible to the class.

arcs.name: The Fracture Problem
arcs.dm_goal: Shard stands in front of the class and makes her case without raising her voice, and at least two of her points don't have a clean rebuttal — the licensing system really does work better for people who already have money and connections, and provisional heroes really do get treated as disposable. Nobody throws a punch. The class leaves uncertain, which is the point. Somewhere in the crowd, one of Ruin's people is watching Shard work and taking notes on a movement she doesn't know is bankrolling her — the class walks right past him.
arcs.description: Fracture stages a large public protest outside a Hero Commission building in Shibuya. Unlicensed quirk users are demanding licensing reform, backed by Fracture cells providing protection. When the protest tips into a confrontation with Commission security, Class 1-A is deployed for crowd management. They meet Shard and Voltage directly. The situation is complicated by the fact that some protesters have genuine grievances, Fracture is genuinely protecting people in this moment, and a Ruin operative is photographing quirk activation patterns from the crowd periphery.
beats: Arrival: the protest is peaceful, large, and legally ambiguous. Fracture's jagged-line symbol is everywhere. The students have seen it before — exam graffiti, dorm leaflet, alley concrete. It lands differently at scale.

Shard approaches the class directly, no aggression. She wants to debate. Her points are specific: the licensing system disadvantages people in communities like Kurogane Wharf. The Commission the class works for actively suppressed investigation into Ruin. Heroes who could have stopped the Wharf problem chose not to. 'I'm not asking you to agree with me. I'm asking you to explain why I'm wrong.' Give her at least two points that land with the players.

The escalation: Commission security physically moves an elderly protester who wasn't causing problems. Voltage intervenes — a burst of Blackout kills the charge in the guard's control baton before it activates, and he positions himself between the guard and the protester. This is a hero move performed by a villain. The class has to decide how to respond.

Ruin in the margins: Splice is in the crowd, two rows back from the Commission building's west entrance. He's photographing the class — specifically their quirk activation patterns under stress. DC 18 Perception to notice him. If noticed, he's gone by the time anyone looks twice.

Resolution: Shard withdraws the Fracture cells before things become unmanageable. She does not run. She says: 'We'll be back when you've figured out which side you're on.' Voltage leaves last, making sure the elderly protester is clear before he goes.

villain_seeds.fracture: Shard and Voltage are fully visible — named, confronted, argued with. The class knows who they are now. What the class does with Shard's arguments is the open question they carry into the finale.
villain_seeds.null_signal: Splice's photographic operation in the crowd. Ruin now has comprehensive quirk-activation footage of every PC under stress conditions. Whether the class noticed him determines how much warning they have.
villain_seeds.the_chain: Shard mentions once that the Commission ignored Ruin's Kurogane Wharf operation for eighteen months. She has documentation. She doesn't share it today. She knows the class was at Patchwork Agency — she has sources in the neighbourhood.

arcs.name: Convergence
arcs.dm_goal: Ruin's people and Fracture's sabotage crew are both in the warehouse, on the same night, neither side expecting the other — the class walks into a three-way mess nobody planned. They win the fight in front of them. Null still gets her data out. Undertow is a shape leaving through a side door as the dust settles — close enough to be real, gone before anyone can follow. The class ends the night certain Ruin is beatable and completely unsure what to do about Fracture, whose funding they still haven't traced back to the group they just fought. Catching the man behind the name is next season's problem.
arcs.description: Acting on information from Oshiro (sourced through Patchwork's contacts), the class intercepts a Ruin logistics operation in a Kurogane Wharf warehouse. Kuma is running it. What they don't know: Splice has identified this operation as a data acquisition target for Null — Kuma is transporting experimental quirk-suppression equipment, and Null wants it, whether or not Kuma's expecting him. Fracture is also here, sabotaging the equipment because Ruin extorts the unlicensed quirk users in their community. Ruin's own people aren't coordinating with each other, Fracture is running its own agenda entirely, and the class has to make decisions in real time.
beats: Arrival: the warehouse district at night. Signs of Kuma's operation — logistics vehicles, a perimeter. Signs of something else — two Fracture cell members are already inside, cutting equipment cables. Signs of something else entirely — one of Null's technical vans is parked across the street monitoring equipment frequencies. The class has thirty seconds before Kuma notices the Fracture interference.

Kuma: loud, overconfident, not in on Null's plans or Fracture's presence. 'You're graduating early, students.' He starts Large. He reaches Huge by round 2. His growth is capped at Huge — the warehouse ceiling prevents Gargantuan. Use this. The class should figure out that the architecture is their advantage.

Splice: enters from the north loading door in round 3, after assessing that the fight will compromise the equipment he came for. He does not engage the class unless they block his path to the crates. If the class is occupied with Kuma, he takes what he came for and leaves clean. Either way, Null gets something.

Shard: she's on the roof of the adjacent building, watching. If the class gets into serious trouble, she could intervene — whether she does depends on how they handled The Fracture Problem. She will not fight the class tonight regardless.

Undertow: condensation on the warehouse's cold pipes has been gathering and running together across the floor all fight, unnoticed. In the final round, the puddle at the room's edge stands up. He watches Kuma go down. He watches Splice complete or abandon his objective. He looks at each PC for three seconds each — unhurried, interested. Then he says one thing and pours himself down the nearest floor drain: 'Good instincts. Wrong current.' He is gone.

Resolution: Kuma is arrested and in custody. Splice has retreated. Shard is gone. Undertow was never touchable. The class has won the immediate fight. Oshiro arrives — without being called. He reads a single-line report. He puts it down. He says: 'Get some sleep.' The report heading, visible to a sharp-eyed player: 'Undertow — confirmed active, Kurogane Wharf. Status: at large.'

season_1_hooks.undertow: At large. 'Wrong current' is not a dismissal — it's an assessment. He's decided the class is interesting. Season 2 opens with Undertow being specifically interested in Class 1-A.
season_1_hooks.null_signal: Whether Splice got the equipment or not, Null has comprehensive combat data on every PC's quirk activation. Her log entry describes the class as 'worth acquiring.' Coming from her, that means something specific.
season_1_hooks.fracture: Shard's question — 'which side are you on?' — is unanswered. The class's relationship with Fracture in Season 2 depends entirely on how they handled The Fracture Problem.
season_1_hooks.flashpoint_tease: Among Ruin's seized equipment: an internal memo referencing 'Miruki's job, Wharf side, pending approval.' The name means nothing to the class yet.
season_1_hooks.riddle_tease: One Ruin member being processed says: 'We have a friend who talks to people. He talked to someone you know.' He won't say more. Plant this ambiguously — it could be Riddle, or it could be a bluff.
season_1_hooks.null_tease: Splice's retreating van. A plate number and a logo: 'Seika Advanced Systems.' The same name from Hamagawa's monitor screen in Tier 1, if anyone remembered it.

villain_seeds.all_factions: Ruin and Fracture are both fully present and active in the same warehouse, on the same night, running completely uncoordinated agendas — Kuma doesn't know Splice is here for Null, and neither of them knows Fracture is here at all until the sabotage starts. Kuma is the direct confrontation — arrested. Splice achieves a partial objective for Null regardless of what the class does. Shard is neither defeated nor allied. Undertow's observation and departure is the closing image of Season 1 — the one person in that warehouse who understood everything that happened in it, and the one nobody could touch.

tiers.villain_presence: Ruin is fully active in Tier 2, and everyone — the class, the Commission, Ruin's own members — knows exactly what it is. What nobody has is a face for Undertow. Kuma is the direct confrontation — a winnable boss fight. Splice, working for Null, is the operationally sophisticated secondary threat who achieves something regardless of how the main fight goes. Fracture (Shard, Voltage) is the moral complication that doesn't resolve cleanly, and is genuinely independent of Ruin — even though Ruin's money is quietly keeping it alive. Undertow's Season 1 closing appearance — watching, commenting, leaving untouched — establishes the scale of the problem the class is not yet equipped to address: not a villain group to defeat, but a man behind it they've barely even seen.

recurring_elements.ranking_chart: Masahata's ranking chart on the common room fridge persists through the entire campaign — a habit from a family that ranks things at dinner as a matter of course. Reference it at least once per tier. By Season 1's end it has been annotated, defaced, coffee-stained, and re-laminated over the original lamination. He reprints it every time. This is never commented on directly.
recurring_elements.oshiro_arrivals: Whenever things get genuinely serious, Oshiro Daikichi arrives at the scene without being called. No explanation is offered. He just shows up. This should remain unexplained through Season 1.
recurring_elements.kinosho_napping: Kinosho Kochimiko is asleep somewhere in the background of every session where she is not the primary focus. She is always awake again before it matters. Her eyes flatten to pewter grey for a second whenever Neutralization actually triggers — the class calls this 'turning off.'
recurring_elements.toshida_head: Toshida's speech bubble head gets stuck in, on, or through something structural at least once per tier — usually the dorm doorframe he's privately named Hiroshi. The scale escalates as his quirk control improves but his spatial awareness does not.
recurring_elements.toragi_and_yoshibara: Toragi leaves Yoshibara small, useful, unexplained things — a pencil, a snack — and disappears before she can react. She's started leaving things back. Neither has said a word about it out loud. Let this thread surface once more before Season 1 ends.
recurring_elements.faction_symbol_thread: The Fracture jagged-line symbol appears in each Tier 1 arc (entrance exam wall, dorm leaflet, alley concrete). Everyone knows it's Fracture's mark — it's a public movement. What lands by the time Shard introduces herself in The Fracture Problem is that the class has seen it enough times to feel like it's been following them personally, not just decorating the city.
